activities.anchor: you subtract the overlap because counting both
activities.caption: the grammar — pair each rule with its clause
activities.name: bayRuleMatch

config.prompt: Match each rule or event pair to its clause:

pairs.left: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
pairs.right: the overlap is subtracted because counting both events counts their intersection twice
the overlap is empty — a card cannot be a heart and a spade
one tells you nothing about the other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)
the second draw is conditional on the first: (4/52) × (3/51) ≈ 0.0045

config.why: Every real gambler's fallacy is a violation of one of these rules — usually treating dependent events as independent.

activities.anchor: after a run of heads, tails is due
activities.caption: coins vs cards — drag the divider to the memory
activities.name: bayMemoryCompare

config.prompt: Two randomisers, one difference — drag the divider:

before.label: coins
before.text: no memory — the sixth flip is still ½; the long-run 50/50 emerges from many flips, not from any self-correction

after.label: cards
after.text: remember — draw without replacement and the deck's composition genuinely changes, making the second ace less likely

config.why: 'Due' reasoning works in exactly one place here: dependent events. Cards remember; coins do not.

activities.caption: one line of this tree method is wrong — click it
activities.name: bayTreeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this tree-diagram method is wrong — click it:
lines: Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) — of the world where B happened, the fraction where A also happens.
It is asymmetric by nature — the conditioning direction matters.
P(rain|clouds) is high; P(clouds|rain) is 1, because every rainy day has clouds.
Each path's probability is the sum of its branch probabilities.
To find the probability of reaching any leaf of type X, you sum the paths.
config.correction: Each path's probability is the product along it (the multiplication rule) — the summing happens across paths, not within one.
config.why: Draw the medical-test scenario as a tree and the famous trap solves itself — provided the conditioning direction is right.

activities.caption: call the posterior before the tree does
activities.name: bayPostEst

config.prompt: A 99%-accurate test for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000 returns positive. What is the probability you are ill (%)?
config.why: 99 / 10,098 ≈ 0.98% — about 1 time in 100. The 999,900 healthy produce ~9,999 false positives, drowning the 99 true positives.
config.context: Posterior odds = prior odds × 99, and prior odds were 1 : 9,999.

activities.caption: the sequential update — rebuild the little table
activities.name: baySeqOrder

config.prompt: Repeat positives, in sequence — order the update table:
items: Prior: odds 1 : 9,999 — the base rate itself
First positive: odds × 99 → 1 : 101, a probability of about 0.98%
Second independent positive: × 99 again → odds ≈ 1 : 1.02, about 49.5%
Third positive: roughly 99% — the evidence has converged
config.why: Each round's posterior feeding the next prior is the qualitative behaviour of all scientific inference.

activities.anchor: A coin-flip example with real numbers
activities.caption: which posterior wore the uniform prior?
activities.name: bayBetaTrace

config.prompt: 10 flips, 7 heads — which curve is the posterior under the uniform prior?

curves.label: no prior — a spike at the raw 0.7

config.why: The informative prior is a gentle nudge — mean 0.69 against 0.67 — already fading; feed in 7,000 heads in 10,000 flips and no reasonable prior matters at all.

activities.caption: size the pool of matching innocents
activities.name: bayDnaEst

config.prompt: A 1-in-a-million DNA profile, a country of 60 million. How many people are expected to share it?
config.why: 1 in a million × 60 million ≈ 60 — so with no other evidence the probability of guilt given the match is roughly 1/60 ≈ 1.7%, not 99.9999%.
config.context: Posterior odds = prior odds × the likelihood ratio; the jury's job is the prior.

activities.caption: two ways to be wrong — file the stakes
activities.name: bayLossSort

config.prompt: Every threshold sets a trade — which error costs more here?

items.label: spam filter — losing a job-offer email to the junk folder
fire alarm — sleeping through a real fire
fraud engine — blocking a legitimate customer's payment

config.why: An airport security officer and an oncologist can rationally act differently on identical evidence — their loss tables differ, and the mathematics cannot value outcomes for you.
